query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing 0.1 at.% carbon into a refractory high-entropy alloy during thermomechanical processing will trigger in situ carbide precipitation, thereby enhancing high-temperature yield strength through precipitation hardening while maintaining low density and preserving room-temperature ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a balanced refractory element composition (e.g., Mo, Nb, Re, Ta, W) produced without carbon addition.
generation.intervention: Add 0.1 at.% carbon during alloy synthesis and subject the alloy to a tailored thermomechanical processing routine designed to promote carbide precipitation.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing performed at high temperatures (approximately 800–1000 °C) under tensile (or compressive) loading, alongside characterization at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of fine, uniformly distributed carbide precipitates (such as Ta3C or Nb3C) within the alloy microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation hardening: the fine carbides act as obstacles to dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, leading to an increase in yield strength, while the low amount of carbon ensures that room-temperature ductility is not compromised and the density remains low.
generation.predicted_outcome: At high temperatures, the RHEA with 0.1 at.% C is expected to exhibit an improvement in yield strength (on the order of a 20–30% enhancement relative to the undoped alloy) without a significant reduction in room-temperature ductility or a meaningful increase in density.
generation.baseline: The same refractory high-entropy alloy produced without any carbon addition.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects depend on precise thermomechanical processing parameters; deviations causing excessive carbide coarsening or non-uniform distribution may lead to embrittlement or failure to enhance high-temperature strength.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the yield strength enhancement and the precipitate distribution may vary with slight differences in alloy chemistry and processing conditions, which necessitates careful optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of a selected refractory high-entropy alloy: one set produced with the standard composition (without carbon) and a second set with an addition of 0.1 at.% carbon. Apply identical thermomechanical processing conditions to both sets. Analyze the microstructure using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to confirm the presence and distribution of carbide precipitates in the C-doped samples. Perform high-temperature mechanical testing (tensile or compressive) at approximately 800–1000 °C as well as room-temperature tests to assess yield strength, ductility, and density.
measurements: Density (via rule of mixtures or experimental measurement)
Microstructural characterization (carbide precipitate identification and distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the C-doped samples do not exhibit fine, uniformly distributed carbide precipitates and fail to demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than ~20% increase) in high-temperature yield strength relative to the undoped samples, while maintaining comparable room-temperature ductility and density, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: With the development of high-temperature metallic materials, Ni-based superalloys have been unable to meet the requirements of aerospace engines. It is urgent to find a new high-performance alloy to replace the Ni-based superalloy []. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) based on refractory elements with superior high-temperature mechanical properties have recently attracted intensive research attention, which are regarded as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials [,,]. However, their inferior plasticity along with high ductile–brittle transition temperature and high density seriously limits their aerospace applications, where the requirements are mainly focus on the deformability and high specific strength of alloys.

In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.

reading.lever: Introduce 0.1 at.% C to trigger in situ carbide precipitation during thermomechanical processing.
reading.why: This approach, adapted from refractory HEA studies, can enhance high-temperature strength via precipitate hardening while adding negligible density and preserving room-temperature ductility.
